catalog_quote: [Valenzuela, Márquez Pinedo & Maddieson 2001:282, 'Stress'] Stress must be considered distinctive in Shipibo, although there are strong regularities. For example, in bisyllabic nouns stress regularly falls on the second syllable if that is closed or has an underlying nasalized vowel, otherwise it falls on the first: e.g. /ˈβawa/ 'parrot', vs. /mɯ̃ˈtsis/ 'nail', /mãˈʂã/ 'heron' or, by a productive process, /βaˈwã/ 'parrot (ergative)'. However, there are exceptions to this pattern, such as /poˈpo/ 'cocona fruit', /taˈsa/ 'basket (kind)', /kaˈpɯ/ 'alligator'. ... [Elias-Ulloa 2006:18, (13)] "Main stress is restricted to occur on one of the two initial syllables of a PrWd. Stress the second syllable if it has a long vowel or it is a closed syllable. Otherwise stress the initial one. Monosyllabic roots with long vowels are always stressed." ... [p.19 fn.3] Putting aside the case of monosylla…
sweep_summary: Shipibo-Conibo is in the catalog as weight-hedged (Valenzuela, Márquez Pinedo & Maddieson 2001 JIPA p.282 plus Elías-Ulloa 2006 Rutgers dissertation, both held). this search of works with stress in the title listed two stress-titled items, both already in our bibliography and both unavailable: (1) Elías Ulloa 2000 'El acento en shipibo' (UNMSM thesis, 158 pp.) is not digitized anywhere reachable (ALICIA searched cleanly with no thesis hit; Cybertesis is a JS shell; RENATI/LA Referencia are behind Anubis; Google Books and OpenAlex quotas exhausted; (2) Loriot 1960 'Shipibo stress and intonation' (SIL Información de Campo 176 microfiche) is absent from the 2016 archived sil.org listing of Loriot's 15 online items and has no URL in Glottolog, so it is microfiche-only, priority low because Loriot's 1993 dictionary sketch p.19 (held) states the rule. New in this search of works with stress in the title: the ALICIA/Dialnet trail led to Elías Ulloa's open-access companion article of the same year, 'El peso silábico en shipibo, en hebreo tiberiano y en kashimiri' (Lengua y Sociedad 3:50-81, 2000), downloaded after solving the journal host's Anubis proof-of-work, scanned (image-only scan) and read: p.56 states first-hand that stress goes to the second syllable if it is CVC, otherwise to the first, with coda-driven stress shifts under /-N/ (p.57) and a footnote showing vowel length alone does not attract stress. It confirms the catalog's classification and does not supersede the deciding sources. with and updated.

new_statements.quote: El shipibo distingue entre sílabas ligeras y pesadas para la asignación del acento. El acento en esta lengua es asignado a la segunda sílaba de la izquierda si ésta es pesada (CVC), de otro modo el acento aparece sobre la primera sílaba. A continuación, mostramos algunos ejemplos representativos de esta sensibilidad al peso silábico. [...] En (4), vemos que el acento se asigna a la sílaba pesada (CVC). Cuando no hay ninguna sílaba pesada, el acento aparece en la sílaba ligera que está más a la izquierda, como en (5).
new_statements.translation: Shipibo distinguishes between light and heavy syllables for stress assignment. Stress in this language is assigned to the second syllable from the left if it is heavy (CVC); otherwise stress appears on the first syllable. Below we show some representative examples of this sensitivity to syllable weight. [...] In (4) we see that stress is assigned to the heavy (CVC) syllable. When there is no heavy syllable, stress appears on the leftmost light syllable, as in (5).
new_statements.citation: Elías Ulloa, José Alberto. 2000. El peso silábico en shipibo, en hebreo tiberiano y en kashimiri. Lengua y Sociedad (Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos) 3: 50-81. DOI 10.15381/lengsoc.v1i3.26431
new_statements.locator: p.56 (PDF p.7), sec. 2.1 'El acento en shipibo'; examples (6) on p.57 (PDF p.8)
new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive stress confined to the first two syllables: second syllable if closed (CVC), otherwise initial; a coda added by /-N/ or removed by resyllabification moves the stress accordingly (/tita/ ['ti.ta] vs [ti.'taN]; /witas/ [wi.'tas] vs ['wi.ta.saN]). Fn. 6 admits further, unpresented aspects (the lexical exceptions of the JIPA account), and fn. 11 gives [mi.'ta.ka.ti] as evidence that a long vowel alone does not attract stress in this analysis. This agrees with the catalog's weight-hedged coding and with the held JIPA 2001, Elías-Ulloa 2006, Valenzuela 2003 and Loriot et al. 1993 statements.

new_statements.quote: The allomorph -t is added to bi-syllable roots ending in an open syllable. With some of these roots, -t triggers a quality change in the last vowel. When a verb stem formed by root-t- precedes a suffix starting with a consonant, the /t/ is deleted and the last vowel of the root gets a compensatory stress. Consider the following examples: meno- 'burn' / meno-t- 'burn oneself' / menó-ke 'burned oneself'; piko- 'take out' / piko-t- 'go out' / pikó-ke 'went out'; choka- 'wash' / chokit- 'wash oneself' / chokí-ke 'washed oneself'; xoka- 'peel' / xokot- 'peel oneself' / xokó-ke 'peeled oneself'.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and the held Elías Ulloa 2000 statement (stress on the second syllable if it is closed, otherwise on the first): in /meno-t-ke/ the second syllable is closed by /t/ and takes stress; after /t/-deletion the stress stays on that syllable ([me.nó.ke]), which Valenzuela describes as compensatory stress. It adds one detail (an opaque interaction: a deleted coda still attracts stress) and states no rule of its own; a stress-on-second-syllable form with a surface-open second syllable would look like an exception to the surface weight rule if the underlying /t/ were ignored. Confidence low because the reading is inferred from four forms plus one…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis is a morphosyntactic study with no phonology, orthography-beyond-a-note, or prosody section (chapters: introduction, conceptual framework, major features of SC = case marking, verb inflection, switch-reference, transitivity; then verb classes). Its only statement about stress is morphophonological: when the de-transitivizer /-t/ is deleted before a consonant-initial suffix, the root-final vowel, i.e. the second syllable of the word, carries stress (menó-ke, pikó-ke, chokí-ke, xokó-ke), which Valenzuela calls 'compensatory'. No general rule of word-stress placement is stated; the examples are the only stress-marked forms in the thesis (the practical orthography used elsewhere does not mark stress).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the allomorphs -meet, -(k)oot, -(k)eet, -(k)iit, -kaat are listed without stress comment
new_statements.identity_note: Valenzuela 1997 describes Shipibo-Conibo (her abbreviation SC) from her own fieldwork since 1990 plus Faust 1973, Bardales 1979, ILV materials and Loriot et al. 1993; no particular dialect (Shipibo vs Conibo vs Capanahua-influenced varieties) is singled out. The Elías Ulloa thesis is titled 'El acento en shipibo' (Shipibo proper), per Glottolog.
